content: The National Institutes of Health (NIH) is an agency under the United States Department of Health and Human Services. It serves as the primary federal agency responsible for conducting and supporting biomedical research. While the NIH conducts a significant portion of research internally, a substantial amount of biomedical research in the United States is funded by the NIH but conducted externally, often by universities, medical schools, and other research institutions. The NIH is divided into two main components: the Extramural division, which funds biomedical research conducted outside of the NIH, and the Intramural division, which conducts research directly within NIH facilities. Intramural research is primarily carried out at the NIH's main campus in Bethesda, Maryland, as well as in surrounding communities. Additional NIH facilities include the National Institute on Aging and the National Institute on Drug Abuse in Baltimore, Maryland, and the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences in Research Triangle Park, North Carolina. The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) also operates the Rocky Mountain Laboratories in Hamilton, Montana, with a focus on virology. The NIH traces its origins back to 1887, when it was established as the Laboratory of Hygiene. It was reorganized in 1930 under the Ransdell Act, becoming the National Institute of Health (singular at the time). Today, the NIH comprises 27 separate institutes and centers, as well as the Office of the Director, all of which are part of the Department of Health and Human Services. The primary goal of NIH research is to generate new knowledge that can help prevent, detect, diagnose, and treat diseases and disabilities. This research spans a wide range of conditions, from rare genetic disorders to common illnesses like the common cold. The NIH's mission is to improve health for all people by uncovering new scientific insights. To achieve this, the NIH conducts research in its own laboratories, funds research by non-federal scientists in institutions across the U.S. and internationally, trains research investigators, and promotes the dissemination of medical and health sciences information. The NIH is composed of numerous specialized institutes, each focusing on specific areas of health and disease. These include the National Cancer Institute (NCI), the National Eye Institute (NEI), the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI), the National Institute on Aging (NIA), the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), the National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS), the National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering (NIBIB), the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD), the National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD), the National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research (NIDCR), the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA), the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS), the National Institute of General Medical Sciences (NIGMS), the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS), the National Institute of Nursing Research (NINR), and the National Library of Medicine (NLM). In addition to its institutes, the NIH includes several centers, such as the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), the Center for Information Technology (CIT), the Center for Scientific Review (CSR), the John E. Fogarty International Center (FIC), the National Center for Complementary and Alternative Medicine (NCCAM), the National Center on Minority Health and Health Disparities (NCMHD), the National Center for Research Resources (NCRR), the Quality Assurance Review Center (QARC), the Warren Grant Magnuson Clinical Center (CC), and the Radiological Physics Center (RPC). The Office of the Director (OD) serves as the central administrative office of the NIH. It is responsible for setting policies, planning, managing, and coordinating the programs and activities of all NIH components. The OD includes program offices that focus on specific research areas, such as minority health, women's health, AIDS research, disease prevention, and behavioral and social sciences research. These offices also provide funding for research through the NIH institutes. Key offices within the OD include the Office of Extramural Research (OER), which oversees research and training programs conducted through grants, contracts, and cooperative agreements; the Office of Intramural Research (OIR), which coordinates research conducted directly by NIH personnel; the Office of Management (OM), which handles management and financial functions; the Office of Administration (OA), which advises on administrative policies and oversees areas such as information resources, grant administration, and procurement; the Office of AIDS Research (OAR), which develops scientific policy and allocates resources for AIDS research; the Office of Behavioral and Social Sciences Research (OBSSR), which advises on research related to human behavior and its impact on health; the Office of Communications and Public Liaison (OCPL), which communicates NIH policies and research findings to the public; the Office of Community Liaison (OCL), which fosters collaboration between the NIH and its community; the Office of Disease Prevention (ODP), which coordinates research on disease prevention and medical practice; the Office of Intramural Training and Education (OITE), which provides guidance on postdoctoral training opportunities; the Office of Equal Opportunity and Diversity Management (OEODM), which advises on equal employment opportunity programs; the Office of Financial Management (OFM), which oversees financial management and budgetary controls; the Office of Human Resources (OHR), which manages human resource programs; the Office of Portfolio Analysis and Strategic Initiatives (OPASI), which helps manage NIH's scientific portfolios and identifies emerging scientific opportunities; and the Office of Research on Women's Health (ORWH), which focuses on improving women's health through research. The Office of Science Education (OSE) coordinates science education activities at the NIH and develops educational resources for students, teachers, and the public. These resources include free curriculum supplements and an interactive career exploration website called LifeWorks, aimed at middle and high school students. The OSE also provides access to other educational materials from across the NIH.
